title: The Reservation Inflation of Hard Money: Gold-Standard Deflation and the Real Expansion of Nominal Claims, 1873-1896
summary: This paper tests the 'reservation inflation' side of the SCR (Scarcity-Circulation-Reservation) monetary theory framework using the 1873-1896 gold-standard deflation period. Using British retail price data and historical U.S. CPI series, the author shows that despite negative circulation inflation (prices fell), fixed nominal claims increased in real value by 22.4% in Britain and 44.0% in the U.S.
key_points: SCR theory posits two forms of inflation: circulation inflation (rising transaction prices) and reservation inflation (rising real value of nominal claims relative to goods)
During 1873-1896, Britain saw price index decline from 18.0 to 14.7 and a 22.4% rise in reservation index
During 1873-1896, U.S. CPI fell from 36.0 to 25.0 with a 44.0% rise in reservation index
The gold-standard deflation period combined negative circulation inflation with positive reservation inflation
Author concludes hard money does not eliminate inflationary pressure but changes its domain of expression
Supports a phase-dependent view of inflation where CPI is only one observable expression of monetary-material asymmetry
why_it_matters: This paper provides historical evidence for an alternative inflation measurement framework (SCR theory) that distinguishes between price-level inflation and claim-value inflation. It challenges the assumption that commodity money systems eliminate inflationary pressure, instead suggesting such pressure manifests in different forms. For archival purposes, the work offers a rigorous test of a non-mainstream monetary theory using 19th-century gold-standard data.

The paper's relevance lies in its contribution to monetary economics research and its implications for how inflation is conceptualized, rather than in providing current macro analysis.
